title: Writing Surveys That Work
intro: Three habits make survey data usable. Each is cheap; skipping them is how a whole survey's data ends up unusable.

learn.title: 1 · Pretest the survey
learn.text:
Run it with a few people **thinking aloud** — moderated over video if you can.

In Calabro's real-estate example, pretesting exposed jargon participants misread and questions they interpreted differently — before the real launch, where there was no room for a redo.

A survey is a one-shot instrument. That's exactly why it needs a usability test.

try.q: Why does a survey need a pretest more than most artefacts?
options: There's no chance to fix it after launch
Surveys are harder to write than tasks
Respondents can't ask anyone for clarification

learn.title: 2 · Know your item type
learn.text:
**Attributes** — who they are. Segment, don't stereotype; ask only when the segment will genuinely change a design decision.
**Behaviours** — what they do. Analytics may be a better source.
**Abilities** — what they can do or know.
**Sentiments** — what they think, feel or judge.

The structure of a good question depends on which kind of information it is meant to collect.

try.q: You want to know how often people use a feature. What's usually the better source?
try.explain: Self-reported frequency is unreliable when the data exists.

right.label: Watch out
items: Only if it changes a decision

learn.title: 3 · Pair the important questions
learn.text:
Add a **“why”** after the rating questions that matter.

A score tells you where you stand; the open follow-up tells you what to do about it. Pairing the two is the cheapest way to turn a number into an action — and it's what makes a one-question pop-up worth running at all.

try.q: What does pairing a rating with an open “why” achieve?
options: It turns a number into something actionable
It allows statistical comparison between groups
try.explain: The score locates the problem; the comment explains it.

test.q: How should a pretest be run?
options: With a few people thinking aloud
By a second researcher reviewing the wording
By testing both versions against each other
test.explain: Moderated over video if you can.

test.q: What did pretesting reveal in the real-estate example?
test.explain: Both would have ruined the data at launch.

test.q: When should you ask an attribute question?
options: When the segment will change a design decision
When the sample is large enough to split by segment

test.q: What are the four item types?
test.explain: Each needs a different question structure.

test.q: Which habit is cheapest to skip and most costly to have skipped?
test.explain: An unusable dataset can't be fixed afterwards.
